subject: Agriculture
title: Agricultural Subsidies
description: A micro-lesson that makes Agricultural Subsidies usable.

hook.text: Rich countries spend $540 billion per year subsidizing agriculture. The money shapes what the world eats.

buildup.text: EU and US subsidies flow mostly to large farms growing corn, wheat, soybeans, and sugar—not fruits or vegetables.

discovery.text: Subsidies keep commodity prices artificially low, making processed food cheap and healthy food comparatively expensive.

twist.text: Subsidized US and EU exports undercut farmers in developing countries who can't compete with below-cost imports.

climax.text: Only 1% of US agricultural subsidies support fruit and vegetable production. The incentives are backwards.

punchline.text: We subsidize what makes us sick and tax what keeps us healthy.

quiz.question: How much do rich countries spend annually on agricultural subsidies?

details.summary: Agricultural subsidies are government payments that support farmers' incomes and stabilize food prices. This topic covers the rationale, scale, and controversy of farm subsidies, including how they distort trade and disadvantage farmers in developing countries.
details.whyItMatters: Rich countries spend over $500 billion annually on agricultural subsidies. These payments shape what gets grown, who can compete in global markets, and whether food systems become more or less sustainable.
takeaways: The US and EU together spend hundreds of billions annually on farm support programs
Subsidies often favor large farms and commodity crops over small and diverse operations
Developing country farmers cannot compete with subsidized exports from rich nations

faq.question: Why do governments subsidize agriculture?
faq.answer: Governments subsidize agriculture to stabilize farmer incomes against volatile markets, ensure domestic food supply, maintain rural economies, keep food prices affordable for consumers, and preserve farmland from development.

faq.question: How do agricultural subsidies harm developing countries?
faq.answer: Subsidized exports from wealthy nations undercut local farmers in developing countries who cannot compete on price, depressing rural incomes, discouraging investment in local agriculture, and increasing dependency on food imports.
